short: China's last dynasty: Manchu rulers, vast expansion, and collapse in 1912.
full:
Hong Taiji proclaimed the Qing at Shenyang in 1636, renaming the Jurchen state his father Nurhaci had built; the dynasty is dated from there rather than from 1644, when Manchu armies entered a Beijing that a rebel had already taken from the Ming. The Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong emperors ruled for 133 years between them, annexing Taiwan, Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang, roughly doubling the territory held under the Ming while the population passed 400 million.

The nineteenth century went badly. Defeat in the Opium Wars brought treaty ports and extraterritoriality; the Taiping rebellion may have killed twenty million; the Boxer settlement imposed an indemnity payable for thirty-nine years. Reform came too late and too slowly. After the Wuchang uprising of October 1911 most provinces declared independence, and on 12 February 1912 the Empress Dowager Longyu abdicated for the six-year-old Puyi, ending both the dynasty and two thousand years of imperial rule in China.
